645.title: Only one arrow
645.hook: the untaught feel pain and then a second arrow of distress (SN 36.6)
645.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use the arrow simile in teaching about pain and illness, and some modern mindfulness programs for chronic pain draw on the distinction between physical pain and the distress added to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the nun Vajira and her chariot, and your line, only suffering comes to be. Today, a teaching from year one, the second arrow, read whole, with the part people usually skip.

You stub your toe on the bed frame at six in the morning. That's the pain. Then, within half a second: who put this bed here, why does this always happen to me, this whole day is ruined. And then, if you're like a lot of people, you reach for something to make it go away: your phone, a snack, an hour of a show. Three moves, one tiny injury. The second arrow may be familiar from year one. But the discourse it comes from keeps going past the second arrow, to that third move.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE AT SIX A.M.` → `THIS ALWAYS HAPPENS TO ME.` → `THEN, REACHING FOR THE PHONE.`

segments.voice: SN 36.6 is called the Arrow. The Buddha asks the monks: the untaught person feels pleasant, painful and neutral feelings. So does the well-taught disciple. What's the difference? Then the picture. Touched by a painful feeling, the untaught person sorrows, grieves, laments, beats their chest, and becomes distraught. So they feel two feelings, one in the body and one in the mind. It's as if a man were struck by an arrow, and then a second arrow hit him in the same place. Here's the part that's often skipped. Touched by pain, the text says, the untaught person seeks delight in sensual pleasure. Why? Because they know no other way out of painful feeling. So pain leads to resistance, resistance leads to reaching for pleasure, and the pleasure feeds a habit of wanting. The discourse names three underlying tendencies stirred up along the way: toward aversion, toward lust, and toward not seeing clearly. A whole cycle, from one stubbed toe. The well-taught disciple, touched by the same pain, doesn't sorrow, lament or become distraught. They feel one feeling, the bodily one. One arrow. And because they know another way out of pain than pleasure, they don't need to reach. Notice what the text doesn't promise. The first arrow still lands, even on the well-taught. The body still hurts. What changes is everything that usually comes after.
screen: `THE SAME FEELINGS, A DIFFERENT RESPONSE` · `A SECOND ARROW IN THE SAME PLACE` · `NO OTHER WAY OUT BUT PLEASURE` · `THE FIRST ARROW STILL LANDS` · then, large: `ONLY ONE ARROW.`

segments.voice: Find one small discomfort in the body right now, a tight back, a restless leg, and feel it plainly: where it is, its size, whether it pulses or stays; that's the first arrow. Watch for the second, a thought like I hate this, and for the third, the urge to fix it with something nice. If either comes, notice it, and come back to just the sensation.

Salla. The Pali word for an arrow or dart, the image in SN 36.6: the well-taught feel the body's pain without the second arrow of distress, and without reaching for pleasure as the only way out. Today's word.
Your line: one arrow lands, not two. The body may still hurt; the rest is what can change. See you tomorrow.

646.title: Foam on the river
646.hook: form like foam, feeling like bubbles, perception a mirage, formations a hollow stalk, consciousness a magic show (SN 22.95)
646.howItsDone: Some Buddhists contemplate the five aggregates through images like these, and teachers in several traditions use the foam, the bubble and the mirage to teach impermanence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the arrow, read whole, and your line, one arrow lands, not two. Today the Buddha sits by the Ganges and points at the water.

The Buddha is staying at Ayojjha, on the bank of the Ganges. The river is carrying a big lump of foam downstream. He tells the monks: suppose someone with good eyes looked closely at that foam, examined it carefully. What would they find? Empty, hollow, nothing solid inside. Then, one after another, he names four more things a person might see in an ordinary year. Five pictures.
screen: `ON THE BANK OF THE GANGES.` → `A LUMP OF FOAM, FLOATING BY.` → `LOOK CLOSELY: WHAT'S INSIDE?`

segments.voice: SN 22.95 matches each of the five heaps, the parts of a person from Vajira's chariot, to something you can see. Form, the body, is like that lump of foam. Feeling is like a bubble: in autumn, when it rains in big drops, a bubble rises on the water and bursts. Pleasant, painful, neither: up and gone. Perception, the mind's labeling, is like a mirage in the last month of the hot season, shimmering on the road, convincing, not there. Formations, our habits and intentions, are like a banana tree. A man goes looking for heartwood with a sharp axe. He cuts down a big, straight, young plantain trunk and peels it, layer after layer, and finds no heartwood at all. Not even softwood. And consciousness is like a magic show, a trick put on by a conjurer at a crossroads. Someone with good eyes sees through it. Each picture is chosen carefully. Foam has a shape, but you can't build with it. Bubbles last a moment. A mirage really does look like water. The plantain is layers all the way down. And the magic show doesn't say consciousness isn't happening; it says it isn't what it appears to be. The point isn't gloom. One who sees this way, the Buddha says, grows disenchanted, and through dispassion is freed. The closing verse adds a plain reminder: this body, when life, heat and consciousness leave it, lies cast aside, food for others. Foam is still beautiful on a river. You just don't try to hold it.

647.title: The burden
647.hook: the five heaps are the burden; craving is the one who picks it up (SN 22.22)
647.howItsDone: The Bhara Sutta is studied in several Buddhist traditions, and its closing verse is sometimes recited or chanted as a reminder that laying down craving brings ease.

segments.voice: Yesterday: five pictures by the Ganges, and your line, up and gone. Today the same five heaps, as something heavy on your back.

Watch someone come home after a long day. The bag drops off one shoulder onto the floor, the shoes come off, and there's a sound, half sigh, half laugh. The body knows the relief of setting something down before the mind has said a word. Some loads are heavier than a bag, and it's easy to miss how heavy until they're off. The Buddha gave a short teaching at Savatthi built on that moment: what's heavy, who carries it, how it gets picked up, and what it's like to put it down.
screen: `THE BAG HITS THE FLOOR.` → `HALF SIGH, HALF LAUGH.` → `WHAT ARE YOU CARRYING?`

segments.voice: SN 22.22 has four parts, like a riddle with its answers. What is the burden? The five heaps that are clung to: body, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. Not the heaps themselves, but the heaps as grasped, taken as me and mine. Who carries the burden? The person, the Buddha says, this venerable one of such a name and such a family. You, by name. What is taking up the burden? Craving: the thirst that leads to more becoming, delighting here and there, craving for pleasure, for existence, for nonexistence. And what is laying it down? The complete fading away and ending of that same craving, letting it go, being free of it. Then a short verse: the five heaps are burdens indeed, and the person carries them. Picking up the burden is suffering in the world. Putting it down is happiness. So the burden is real, someone carries it, and craving picks it up. Which means the putting down happens there too. Not by throwing away the body or the mind, but by loosening the grip that keeps lifting them. A footnote: an early Buddhist school, the Personalists, pointed to this sutta to argue that the person is real in some sense, since someone carries the burden. Other schools replied that the person here is a conventional name, like the chariot. The debate went on a long time, and Buddhist schools still read the passage differently. What they share is the last line: putting it down is happiness.
screen: `THE BURDEN: THE HEAPS, CLUNG TO` · `THE CARRIER: THIS PERSON, BY NAME` · `PICKING IT UP: CRAVING` · `PUTTING IT DOWN: CRAVING ENDS` · then, large: `PUT IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Notice one thing you're carrying right now, not a bag but a worry, a resentment, a job you've decided only you can do, and feel where it sits: shoulders, chest, jaw. Ask quietly what keeps picking it up; often it's a wanting, to be right, to be safe, to be in control. For these few minutes, let it rest on the floor beside you, knowing you can pick it up later, and feel the shoulders drop.

Your line: put it down. Putting it down is happiness. Day six hundred forty-seven, done.

648.title: The dog on a leash
648.hook: a dog tied to a post circles it endlessly: clinging to self (SN 22.99)
648.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the leash simile to explain identity view, the twenty ways of taking the five aggregates as self, which many traditions treat as the first fetter to be broken.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the burden, and your line, put it down. Today the heaps again, and an animal you've probably seen outside a shop.

Outside a grocery store, a dog is tied to a post. Its person went in five minutes ago. The dog walks one way around the post, then the other, wrapping and unwrapping its leash, sitting, standing, circling again. It's going somewhere and nowhere at once. Everyone who walks past smiles, because it's so clearly waiting for something it can't make happen faster. The Buddha used that very picture, a dog tied to a stake, and he wasn't talking about dogs.
screen: `TIED OUTSIDE THE STORE.` → `ONE WAY AROUND, THEN THE OTHER.` → `GOING NOWHERE, FAST.`

segments.voice: SN 22.99 begins with a large claim. This round of wandering, the Buddha says, has no beginning that can be found. Beings roam on, blocked by not knowing, tied by craving. A time may come when the great ocean dries up, when this great earth is burned up. Even so, the suffering of beings who wander like this doesn't end. Then the picture. Suppose a dog on a leash is tied to a strong post or pillar. It just runs and circles around that post. In the same way, the untaught person regards the body as self, or self as having a body, or the body as inside the self, or the self as inside the body. The same with feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. So they circle those five, and aren't freed from them. The post is the heaps. The leash is taking them as me. The dog isn't evil and isn't stupid. It's just tied, and every lap it runs is real: moving, trying, hoping. The circle is set by the post. Those four ways are precise. I am my body. I have a body. My body is in me. I am in my body. The sutta says these are all ways of being tied. The good news is in the same picture. A dog that isn't tied doesn't circle. The text, here and in the next discourse, goes on: one who doesn't take the heaps as self isn't bound to the post.

segments.voice: Notice one thought you keep circling, a worry about money, something someone said, and watch it come around again, the way the dog comes round the post. 649.title: More than the oceans
649.hook: the tears shed over countless lives are more than the four oceans (SN 15.3)
649.howItsDone: Buddhist communities mark grief in many ways, with chanting, merit-making and memorial rites for the dead, and teachings like the tears and the oceans are sometimes shared at funerals and in times of loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dog circling its post, and your line, round and round. Today the Buddha asks the monks a question about water, and the answer is tears.

A hard cry has a shape. Where you were sitting. What the light looked like. The way it came in waves, and how tired the body was after. A death, maybe, or a breakup, or a phone call. In the middle of it, a loss can seem like the only one in the world. In a short chapter of the Connected Sayings about the long round of lives, the Buddha takes that one private cry and sets it beside a very large body of water.
screen: `A HARD CRY HAS A SHAPE.` → `IT COMES IN WAVES.` → `BESIDE A VERY LARGE WATER.`

segments.voice: SN 15.3 is a question and answer. The Buddha asks the monks: which is more? The tears you have shed while wandering this long round, weeping and wailing because you were joined with what you disliked and parted from what you loved, or the water in the four great oceans? The monks answer from what they've been taught: the tears, sir. The tears are more. Yes, the Buddha says, and he names them one by one. For a long time you have suffered the death of a mother. The tears shed over that alone are more than the four oceans. The death of a father. A brother. A sister. A son. A daughter. The loss of relatives, of wealth, the suffering of illness. Each time, the same refrain: more than the water in the four great oceans. It's a hard teaching to sit with, and the text doesn't soften it. But notice its tone. It isn't scolding anyone for crying. It's almost tender: you've lost so much, for so long. It takes grief seriously enough to measure it against the sea. Then it draws a conclusion: enough. Reason enough to grow weary of the round, to let the craving that keeps it turning fade, and to be free. Buddhists hold the idea of many lives in different ways. Some take rebirth literally; some modern teachers read it more as moment to moment. Either way, the picture makes one point plainly: in this teaching, no grief is the first.

650.title: No beginning to find
650.hook: count your mothers with twigs, your fathers with balls of clay, and the earth runs out first (SN 15.1–2)
650.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism especially, students practice recognizing all beings as having once been their mothers, as a basis for compassion; teachers in other traditions draw on the same chapter of the Samyutta Nikaya.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tears and the four oceans, and your line, be gentle with grief. Today the same chapter opens, with grass and clay and a counting game no one can finish.

Send off a sample of your spit, and you can get back a map of where your great-great-grandparents lived. Go back far enough, though, and the branches multiply faster than anyone can count. Two parents, four grandparents, eight, sixteen, and soon the chart is wider than the page. The Buddha starts the chapter on the long round of lives with a family tree too. But instead of paper, he uses all the grass in India, and then the whole earth.
screen: `A FAMILY TREE BY MAIL.` → `TWO, FOUR, EIGHT, SIXTEEN.` → `NOW USE ALL THE GRASS.`

segments.voice: SN 15.1 opens with a sentence the rest of the chapter keeps returning to. This round of wandering, monks, is without a discoverable beginning. No first point can be found where beings, blocked by not knowing and tied by craving, started roaming. Suppose someone cut all the grass, sticks, branches and leaves in India, gathered them in one heap, and cut them into little sticks four fingers long. Then, laying them down one at a time, they counted: this is my mother, this is my mother's mother. The grass and sticks of India would run out before the line of mothers did. SN 15.2 does the same with the earth. Roll it into balls of clay the size of a jujube seed and lay them down: this is my father, this is my father's father. The earth runs out first. Then the conclusion: for so long you have experienced loss and suffering. It's enough to grow weary of all this, and to be free. The images stretch the mind until it gives up looking for the edge. Not a large number; no number at all. A little later in the same chapter, the Buddha draws out one surprising consequence. It is hard, he says, to find a being who has not at some time been your mother, or your father, your brother, sister, son or daughter. Some Buddhist teachers, in Tibet especially, have built a practice of kindness on that line: anyone you meet may once have been family.

what it means: in SN 15.1–2, the round of lives has no discoverable beginning; the grass and the earth run out before the line of mothers and fathers.

what a scholar hears: anamatagga is rendered 'whose first point is not known'; the same chapter's line that it is hard to find a being who has not been one's mother is echoed in Tibetan practices for developing compassion.
recall: the way to the far shore

chat.says: Why do some Buddhists say anyone you meet may have been your mother?
options: The round of lives has no findable beginning, so anyone may once have been family.
It's a polite way of reminding people to respect their elders and parents.
Because families are reborn together as a group, life after life.
chat.meaning: SN 15 says the round has no discoverable beginning, so it's hard to find a being who hasn't at some time been your mother or father.

651.title: The whole of it
651.hook: Ananda says good friendship is half the holy life; no, the whole (SN 45.2)
651.howItsDone: Buddhist communities across traditions practice together in sanghas, temples and retreat groups, and teachers often cite this sutta when they speak about spiritual friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: grass, clay and the line of mothers, and your line, anyone may have been family. Today Ananda makes a guess about friendship, and closes the week by being corrected.

A friend drags someone to the gym on a cold morning. Another says, kindly, that a relationship isn't doing them any good. A third just keeps showing up, again and again, until the other person starts showing up too. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, has been thinking about friendship. He comes to the Buddha in a Sakyan town and says, with some confidence, that he's worked out how much good friends are worth. He's about to be told he's off by half.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO GETS YOU THERE.` → `ANANDA HAS A THEORY.` → `OFF BY HALF.`

segments.voice: SN 45.2 is short, with a surprise in the middle. Ananda says: half of the holy life, venerable sir, is good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship. A generous estimate. The Buddha's reply is immediate. Not so, Ananda, not so. Good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship is the entire holy life. When someone has a good friend, he explains, you can expect them to develop the noble eightfold path, right view, right intention, all the way through. A good friend doesn't just help with the path. They're how the path gets walked. Then he points to himself. It's by relying on me as a good friend that beings subject to birth are freed from birth, beings subject to aging, from aging, subject to sorrow, from sorrow. The teacher calls himself a friend. The Pali phrase is kalyanamittata, having a lovely, good friend: kalyana means beautiful, good, and mitta means friend. It doesn't mean someone who agrees with everything. Another discourse in the Numbered Sayings sketches a good friend as one who speaks up, can bear to be spoken to, and doesn't lead you toward what harms. Look back at this week: one arrow instead of two, foam on the river, the burden put down, a dog circling its post, tears more than the oceans, a line of mothers with no beginning. Heavy material, most of it. And the week ends with the Buddha saying the way through all of it is walked with friends.
screen: `HALF THE HOLY LIFE, SAYS ANANDA` · `NOT SO: THE ENTIRE HOLY LIFE` · `THE BUDDHA AS A GOOD FRIEND` · `KALYANAMITTA: A LOVELY FRIEND` · then, large: `THE WHOLE OF IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one good friend, someone who has helped you become a little kinder, a little braver, and remember one specific time they showed up for you. Let gratitude fill the chest without pushing it. Then, if you'd like, hold a simple wish for them: may you be well.
Kalyanamitta. The Pali term for a good or lovely friend, from SN 45.2, where the Buddha tells Ananda that good friendship is not half but the entire holy life. Today's word.
Your line: walked with friends. Not half the path, the whole of it. That's a week.

screen: `DAY 651 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ALL IS BURNING, READ WHOLE.`

fork.setup: you're Ananda. you've thought it through and tell the Buddha good friendship is half the holy life. what does he say?
options: yes, exactly half.
not so: it is the entire holy life.
friendship has nothing to do with it.
fork.reveal: he corrects Ananda at once: good friendship is the whole of the holy life, because with a good friend the path gets walked.

original.note: Pali kalyanamitta: a good or lovely friend; kalyanamittata is good friendship.

trapdoor: what you thought: the whole of it is about being a loyal friend.
what it means: in SN 45.2, good friendship is not half but the entire holy life, because with a good friend one develops the eightfold path.
what a scholar hears: SN 45 is the Magga Samyutta, the chapter on the path; the same exchange appears again in SN 3.18, where the Buddha tells it to King Pasenadi.
recall: a chariot, a name for its parts

chat.says: Is friendship a big deal in Buddhism, or more of a side thing?
options: Ananda guessed half the holy life; the Buddha said good friendship is all of it.
It's about half; the other half is your own effort on the cushion.
Friends matter, but only monks living together count as good friends.
chat.meaning: In SN 45.2 the Buddha corrects Ananda: good friendship isn't half the holy life but the entire holy life.
